title: Tiered Model Selection for a High-Volume Ticket Triage System
description: Tests the ability to tune model tier, prompting technique, context/caching strategy, and guardrail enforcement together for a mixed-workload system, rather than optimizing any one lever in isolation.

scenario.background: A support-ticket triage system processes 50,000 tickets per day. Each ticket needs: (1) classification into one of 12 categories, (2) for tickets classified as "billing dispute," a structured JSON summary against a specific schema pulled from a 40-page billing-policy reference document, and (3) escalation to a human for anything touching an account closure or a refund over $1,000.

characters.name: Tomas Vidal
characters.concern: Wants inference cost under control at 50K tickets/day, without sacrificing accuracy on the cases that actually carry financial risk.

characters.name: Aisha Bello
characters.concern: The $1,000/account-closure escalation rule must never depend on the model choosing to follow a prompt correctly.

questions.stem: Which model-tiering strategy correctly matches Tomas's cost concern to the actual shape of the workload?
options: Use the most capable model tier for all 50,000 tickets/day to guarantee consistent quality

Use a fast, cheap model tier for the narrow, high-volume classification step (1), and route only the subset classified as billing disputes to a stronger model tier for the policy-nuanced structured summary (step 2)
Use the cheapest model tier for every step, including billing-dispute summaries, since cost is the primary concern
Alternate randomly between tiers across all three steps to average out cost and quality
questions.explanation: B is correct because classification is narrow, high-volume, and low-stakes-per-error, which is exactly where a cheap, fast tier optimizes cost without hurting outcomes, while the billing-dispute summary genuinely needs stronger reasoning to apply policy nuance correctly — tiered routing sends only that smaller subset to the stronger tier. A wastes budget on the 88% of tickets that don't need deep reasoning. C risks getting the policy-nuanced summary wrong, which is the step where an error is most costly. D applies no reasoning about which step needs which capability at all.

questions.stem: Which prompting-technique choice best fits step 2 (structured JSON summary against a specific schema, pulled from a 40-page policy document)?
options: Zero-shot with just a description of the desired schema, since the model can infer standard JSON structure
Few-shot examples (2-3 sample tickets with correct structured JSON output) combined with a light chain-of-thought instruction to first identify the relevant policy clause, then populate the summary
Chain-of-thought alone, with no examples, since reasoning step-by-step is sufficient for any structured-output task
Increase sampling temperature to generate more varied possible summaries and pick the best one
questions.explanation: B is correct because a specific, non-obvious schema needs few-shot examples to lock the exact structure, and getting the *policy application* wrong is worse than getting the format wrong — the light CoT instruction (identify the clause first) targets that specific risk. A fails because a zero-shot description alone won't reliably reproduce an exact, non-standard schema. C fails because reasoning without examples doesn't teach the model the exact JSON shape it needs to reproduce. D fails because raising temperature increases output variability, which works against reliably reproducing a fixed schema.

questions.stem: The 40-page billing-policy document and the few-shot examples are identical on every step-2 call, while only the individual ticket text varies. What context/caching strategy best fits this pattern?
options: Place the policy document and few-shot examples before a cache breakpoint, with the varying ticket text placed after it, so the stable prefix is cached and only the per-call ticket text is processed fresh
Skip caching entirely, since the policy document changes too rarely to matter
Cache the ticket text instead, since that's the part sent most frequently
Regenerate the policy document summary fresh on every call to keep it maximally accurate
questions.explanation: A is correct because prompt caching benefits an identical, reused prefix — placing the stable policy document and examples first (and unchanged) before the varying ticket text means the large, repeated portion is served from cache at a fraction of the cost on every call after the first, cutting both cost and latency. B forfeits real, ongoing savings on a stable, frequently-reused prefix. C is backwards — the ticket text is exactly the part that's *not* reused across calls, so caching it provides no benefit. D adds no value since the document doesn't need to be regenerated, only reused.

questions.stem: How should the $1,000/account-closure escalation rule be enforced to satisfy Aisha's requirement that it never depend on the model following a prompt correctly?
options: State the rule clearly in the system prompt ("never process refunds over $1,000 without escalation") and trust the model to comply

Have the structured JSON output from step 2 include an amount field, and enforce a deterministic, code-level check outside the model that routes anything over $1,000 or flagged as account-closure to a human queue regardless of what the model's prose suggests
Ask the model to double-check its own output for compliance with the escalation rule before finalizing
Rely on the human queue reviewing every single ticket regardless of amount, making the automated classification irrelevant
questions.explanation: B is correct because a hard compliance rule needs a deterministic, code-level gate outside the model's judgment — the prompt-level instruction can reduce how often the model even suggests auto-processing such a case, but only a structural check guarantees it never happens silently, which is exactly what Aisha requires. A is a soft control that can be missed or degraded by later prompt changes, which is the failure mode Aisha is trying to prevent. C still relies on the model's own judgment, which is the same weakness as A. D defeats the purpose of the whole triage system by routing everything to humans regardless of risk.

keyLearnings: Model tier, prompting technique, context/caching strategy, and guardrails trade against each other — tuning one in isolation (e.g., picking a cheap model without adjusting the prompting technique) undermines the others.
Tiered routing sends the minority of high-stakes, nuanced work to a stronger model while keeping high-volume, low-stakes work on a cheap, fast tier.
Few-shot examples are the direct fix when a task requires an exact, non-obvious output schema that a model can't reliably infer from a description alone.
A hard compliance rule (like a dollar-amount escalation threshold) must be enforced as a deterministic, code-level check outside the model — a system-prompt instruction alone is not a guarantee.
